The Surah al-Sharh (Al-Inshirah) is Meccan. [Narrated by Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The surah 'Alam nashrah' was revealed in Mecca." Some added: "after the forenoon (al-Duha)." See: al-Durr al-Manthur, 8/547.] In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

* *

﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ That is, did We not open and widen it, and soften your heart with faith, prophethood, knowledge and wisdom.

﴿And We removed from you your burden﴾. Al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: "And We remitted from you what had passed of you in the Jahiliyyah (the Age of Ignorance). It is like His saying: ﴿That Allah may forgive you your past sin and what will follow﴾ [al-Fath: 2]."

Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: it means error and forgetfulness. It was also said: it means the sins of your Ummah, which were attributed to him because his heart was preoccupied with them. ʿAbd al-ʿAziz ibn Yahya and Abu ʿUbayda said: it means We lightened from you the burdens of prophethood and the responsibility of carrying out its affairs.

﴿Which had weighed down your back﴾: it burdened your back, so that it was weakened until a creaking sound was heard from it, that is, a sound.

﴿And We raised for you your mention﴾. Akhbarana Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Shurayhi, akhbarana Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Ibrahim al-Tha'labi, akhbarana Abu al-Qasim ʿAbd al-Khaliq ibn ʿAli al-Mu'adhdhin, haddathana Abu Bakr ibn Habib, haddathana Abu Isma'il Muhammad ibn Isma'il, haddathana Safwan, that is Ibn Salih ʿAbd al-Malik, haddathana al-Walid, that is ibn Muslim, haddathani ʿAbd Allah ibn Lahi'ah from Darraj from Abu al-Haytham from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: that the Prophet (ﷺ) asked Jibril (peace be upon him) about this verse, "And We raised for you your mention." He said: Allah the Exalted says: ﴿When I am mentioned, you are mentioned along with Me﴾. [Narrated by al-Tabari 30/235, Abu Ya'la in al-Musnad 2/131, and Ibn Hibban no. (1772) p. (439) in Mawarid al-Zam'an. It contains Ibn Lahi'ah, who became confused, and Darraj, who is weak.]

And from al-Hasan who said: "And We raised for you your mention" means: when I am mentioned, you are mentioned [along with Me]. ʿAta' said, from Ibn ʿAbbas: it means the adhan, the iqamah, the tashahhud and the khutbah on the pulpits; and if a servant worshipped Allah and affirmed Him in everything but did not testify that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, he would benefit from nothing, and he would be a disbeliever.

Qatadah said: Allah raised his mention in this world and the Hereafter; there is no preacher, no one reciting the tashahhud, and no one in prayer, except that they call out: "I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." [Narrated by al-Tabari 30/235. al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur 8/548–549 added its attribution to ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il.]

al-Dahhak said: no prayer is accepted without it, and no khutbah is valid without it. Mujahid said: "And We raised for you your mention" means by the call to prayer (al-ta'dhin).

Hassan ibn Thabit said regarding this:

Did you not see that Allah sent His servant with His proof, while Allah is higher and more glorious?

Radiant, upon him is the seal of prophethood, from Allah, witnessed, shining and bearing witness.

Allah joined the name of the Prophet with His own name when the muadhdhin says in the five (prayers): "I bear witness."

He split for him a part of His name to honour him, so the Lord of the Throne is Mahmud and this is Muhammad. [See: Diwan of Hassan (may Allah be pleased with him), p. 47, Beirut edition.]

It was also said: Allah raised his mention by taking the covenant from the prophets and obliging them to believe in him and acknowledge his excellence.

Then He promised him ease and relief after hardship, for he had been in hardship in Mecca, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said:

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 94, verses 5–6:

﴿So indeed, with hardship comes ease﴾, that is, with the hardship you are in from fighting the polytheists comes ease and relief, by His making you prevail over them until they submit to the truth you have brought them. "Indeed, with hardship comes ease" is repeated to confirm the promise and magnify the hope.

Al-Hasan said: When this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Rejoice, ease has come to you. One hardship will never overcome two eases" [[Narrated by al-Tabari: 30/235–236, and it is mursal (disconnected in its chain). Al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur: 8/550 also attributed it to Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Mardawayh.]].

Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Were hardship in a hole, ease would seek it out until it entered it. Indeed, one hardship will never overcome two eases" [[Narrated by Abd al-Razzaq in al-Tafsir: 2/380–381, and al-Tabari: 30/236; al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur: 8/550–551 added its attribution to al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh.]].

The exegetes said: The meaning of his saying, "One hardship will never overcome two eases," is that Allah repeated "hardship" with the definite form and "ease" with the indefinite form. It is the custom of the Arabs that when they mention a definite noun and then repeat it, the second is the same as the first; but when they mention an indefinite noun and then repeat it in the same form, it becomes two. And when they repeat it in the definite form, the second is the same as the first. For example, when you say: "If I earn a dirham, I spend a dirham," the second is different from the first; but if you say: "If I earn a dirham, then I spend the dirham," the second is the first. So "hardship" in the verse is repeated in the definite form, so it is one hardship, and "ease" is repeated in the indefinite form [in "B" it reads "the indefinite" (al-nakirah)], so they are two eases. It is as if He said: "Indeed, with hardship comes ease; indeed, with that hardship comes another ease."

Abu Ali [al-Hasan] [[In "A" it reads "al-Husayn," and the correct reading is what I have established.]] ibn Yahya ibn Nasr al-Jurjani, author of "al-Nazm" [[That is, "Nazm al-Qur'an," which is in two volumes. See: the biography of Abu Ali al-Hasan ibn Yahya in "Tarikh Jurjan" by al-Sahmi, pp. 187–188.]], said: People have spoken about his saying, "One hardship will never overcome two eases," and nothing came from them except their saying that hardship is definite and ease is indefinite, so there must be one hardship and two eases. This is a flawed view. If a man says, "Indeed, with the horseman is a sword" [the words in parentheses are omitted in "B"], this does not require that the horseman be one and the sword two. The meaning of His saying, "One hardship will never overcome two eases," is that Allah sent His Prophet (ﷺ) while he was poor and destitute, and the Quraysh used to reproach him for that, until they said: "If what you want is wealth, we will gather wealth for you until you are like the wealthiest people of Makkah." The Prophet was saddened by this and thought that his people were only denying him because of his poverty. So Allah enumerated His blessings upon him in this surah and promised him wealth, to console him for the grief that had entered him. He said: "Indeed, with hardship comes ease." Its meaning: Do not let what they say grieve you, for with hardship comes ease in this world swiftly, then He fulfilled His promise to him, opened for him the Arabian lands, and widened his means, so that he gave hundreds of camels and made splendid gifts. Then He began another favor concerning the matter of the Hereafter, saying: "Indeed, with hardship comes ease." The evidence that it is a new beginning is its being free of a conjunction (fa or wa). This is a promise to all believers. Its meaning: Indeed, with the hardship of this world, there is ease for the believer in the Hereafter. Thus the two eases may gather for him: the ease of this world, which is what He mentioned in the first verse, and the ease of the Hereafter, which is what He mentioned in the second verse. So his saying, peace be upon him, "One hardship will never overcome two eases," means: the hardship of this world will never overcome the ease that He promised the believers in this world and the ease that He promised them in the Hereafter. Only one of them is overcome, namely the ease of this world, whereas the ease of the Hereafter is lasting and does not pass away. That is, the two are not overcome together, as in his saying (ﷺ): "The two festivals of 'Eid are two months that never decrease" [[Narrated by al-Bukhari in al-Sawm: "Two months of 'Eid that never decrease": 4/124; and Muslim in al-Siyam, the explanation of his saying (ﷺ) "Two months of 'Eid that never decrease," no. 1089: 2/766.]], meaning they do not both decrease together.

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 94, verse 7:**

﴿So when you are free, then strive hard﴾. That is, then exert yourself. Nasab (*nasab*, toil, exertion) means toil. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: "When you are free from the obligatory prayer, then strive hard (*fa-nsab*) toward your Lord in supplication, and turn eagerly to Him in asking, and He will give to you." [[Narrated by al-Tabari (Jami' al-Bayan): 30/236. The author of al-Durr al-Manthur (al-Suyuti) added its attribution to 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh: 8/551.]]

[It was related by 'Abd al-Wahhab ibn Mujahid from his father, who said: "When you pray, then exert yourself in supplication and asking."] [[What is between the brackets is missing from manuscript "A".]]

Ibn Mas'ud said: "When you are free from the obligatory duties, then strive hard in the night prayer (*qiyam al-layl*)." [[Attributed by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur (8/551) to Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim.]]

al-Sha'bi said: "When you are free from the tashahhud, then supplicate for your worldly life and your hereafter."

al-Hasan and Zayd ibn Aslam said: "When you are free from fighting your enemy, then strive hard in the worship of your Lord." [[Narrated by al-Tabari: 30/237. See also al-Durr al-Manthur: 8/552.]]

Mansur related from Mujahid: "When you are free from the affairs of this world, then strive hard in the worship of your Lord, and pray." [[Narrated by al-Tabari: 30/237, who, giving preference to a view, said: "The most correct of these sayings is the saying of the one who said: God, may He be remembered, commanded His Prophet to make his freedom from everything with which he was occupied, of his worldly and religious affairs, insofar as that occupation was useful to him, and commanded him, when occupied with it, to exert himself in His worship and in what brings him closer to Him, and in asking Him for his needs. He did not restrict this to a particular state of his freedom rather than another. So every state of his freedom is alike, whether his freedom was from prayer, or from jihad, or from a worldly matter with which he was occupied, because the condition is general, without specifying one state of freedom over another."]]

Hayyan related from al-Kalbi: "When you are free from conveying the message, then strive hard," that is: "Seek forgiveness for your sin and for the believers."

"And to your Lord direct your longing." ʿAṭāʾ said: Humble yourself before Him, fearful of the Fire and desiring Paradise. It is also said: Make your longing directed to Him in all your circumstances. Al-Zajjaj said: That is, make your desire directed to Allah alone.
